title: Whistling!
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck (Chuck is labeled "iHeart Intro" in the transcript) explore whistling: the main whistling styles (pucker, palatal, finger, throat), how to learn to whistle and the physics of the Helmholtz chamber, the history of whistling from prehistoric bone whistles and ancient accounts to vaudeville whistling acts and the decline of whistling with portable music, whistled languages used across mountains and with greater honeyguide birds, wolf whistles, whistling superstitions, whistling in film and songs, whistle register singing, competitive whistling and the Masters of Musical Whistling, record-setting whistles, and a stroke patient who communicated by whistling. Episode closes with listener mail from Jessica Chang about her children's book on New York City trash.
topics: Jessica Chang Gary meets Marge the Barge

entities.name: The Good, the Bad and the Ugly
Agnes Woodward California School of Artistic Whistling

segments.title: Opening banter and whistling defined
segments.summary: Josh introduces the episode on whistling, defining it as forcing air through a narrow passage with pursed lips (pucker whistling). The hosts ask whether they whistle and share office anecdotes.

segments.title: Types of whistling
segments.summary: The hosts go through whistling styles: palatal whistling, finger whistling, and throat whistling, and try to clarify how palatal whistling is done.

segments.title: Throat whistling videos
segments.summary: Chuck recommends YouTube videos of Ralph Whistler doing throat whistling in 1984 on Kelly and Company and a redub parody.

segments.title: Origins of whistling and whistled languages in ancient accounts
segments.summary: Whistling may predate speech as a proto-language. Bone whistles from the Neolithic and possibly Neanderthals suggest early whistling. Herodotus described Ethiopian troglodytes who may have had a whistled language.

segments.title: Off-topic chat: sports, wings and a roast
segments.summary: The hosts digress into chicken wings, a Mastodon drummer encounter, and a critique of the Tom Brady roast.

segments.title: Whistling for pleasure and vaudeville whistling acts
segments.summary: Whistling for pleasure dates back at least to Chaucer and the 1600s. Vaudeville whistlers such as Ronnie Ronalde, who sold out Radio City Music Hall for ten weeks in 1949, were popular. The Agnes Woodward California School of Artistic Whistling opened in 1909 with clients including John Wayne.

segments.title: Decline of whistling and its bad reputation
segments.summary: Whistling declined mid-century, attributed to transistor radios and later Walkmans and iPods. In the UK whistling was associated with pickpockets and thieves, and became a comedic trope of a carefree shoplifter.

segments.title: Whistling as a surviving subculture
segments.summary: Josh compares whistling's revival to roller skating in Black culture. Marge Carlson, a 1990s whistler, released albums where her whistling was an instrument.

segments.title: Contemporary professional and competitive whistlers
segments.summary: Molly Lewis is a professional whistler with an EP called The Forgotten Edge. Competitive whistlers such as Chris Olman and Herbert Chatrow have competed in international whistling finals.

segments.title: Whistling in circus, soundtracks and songs
segments.summary: Whistlers have performed with circus acts; Molly Lewis whistled on the Barbie soundtrack. Ennio Morricone's spaghetti Western theme is whistled by Alessandro Alessandroni. Twisted Nerve from the 1968 thriller is discussed, and Josh attempts to whistle it.

segments.title: Whistling as character voice and emotional expression
segments.summary: Jason Saranas did Woodstock's whistles in Peanuts, and Percy Edwards voiced whistles for animated characters and Fizgig in The Dark Crystal. The hosts discuss whistles as expressions of emotion.

segments.title: Whistled languages and communication with animals
segments.summary: Whistle languages carry over mountains and valleys, traveling about 550 meters versus 40 meters for speech. They mirror spoken language in simplified form. Human honey foragers whistle to the greater honeyguide bird to find beehives in Tanzania and Mozambique.

segments.title: Wolf whistles
segments.summary: The wolf whistle may have started as a shepherd's warning about wolves, later became street harassment. France reportedly banned wolf whistling in 2018 with a fine. Its earliest traced appearance is a 1943 Tex Avery cartoon.

segments.title: Whistling superstitions
segments.summary: Many cultures consider whistling in certain places or times, especially at night or in the dark, to be bad luck, summoning spirits or demons.

segments.title: Break and how to whistle
segments.summary: Break segment transitions into a discussion of how to learn whistling. Covers the tongue position, the Helmholtz chamber resonance, and Chris Olman's four steps.

segments.title: Whistling in movies and famous references
segments.summary: The To Have and Have Not line 'you know how to whistle' is discussed, along with Snow White's whistle while you work and the Andy Griffith Show theme.

segments.title: Whistling songs
segments.summary: The hosts name songs with whistling: Walk Like an Egyptian, Dock of the Bay, Winds of Change, Don't Worry Be Happy, Axl Rose in Patience, and Pixies' Where Is My Mind.

segments.title: Whistle register singing
segments.summary: Mariah Carey and Minnie Riperton are noted for singing in the whistle register, higher than falsetto. Christina Aguilera was also mentioned.

segments.title: Whistling competitions history
segments.summary: The Louisburg College Folk Festival whistling competition started in 1973, ended in 2014, and became the National Whistlers Convention. Caroline Kaufman created the Masters of Musical Whistling in Pasadena in 2020.

segments.title: Whistling world records
segments.summary: Hosts discuss a Guinness record for most people whistling at once (853 at Spring Harvest, UK, 2014) and the idea of breaking it at a live show. They cover loudest whistle records (Marco Ferrara 2004 and Luca Zocchi 2014, 125 decibels) and Joshua Lockert's highest whistle at 10,599 Hz.

segments.title: Whistle register humor and stroke patient case study
segments.summary: The hosts jokingly discuss whistle register abilities. Josh cites a 1984 British Medical Journal case of a stroke patient who communicated by whistling.

segments.title: Listener mail: Jessica Chang's trash book
segments.summary: Listener Jessica Chang writes about her New York City trash obsession and her children's book Gary Meets Marge the Barge, inspired by the garbage barges on the East River.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts invite listeners to write in about their books and the show closes with the iHeartRadio credit.
